vicuna.origin: The vicuna, Vicugna vicugna, is a wild camelid of the high Andes of Peru, Bolivia, Argentina, Chile and Ecuador, and the wild ancestor of the alpaca. Mitochondrial studies separate northern V. v. mensalis and southern V. v. vicugna lineages. Hunted for its fiber for more than 400 years, it was seriously endangered by the end of the 1960s, then recovered to an estimated 275,000 animals by the mid-2000s, and it is now listed as Least Concern by the IUCN. Fiber comes from wild or semi-captive animals that are captured, shorn and released.
vicuna.structure: Vicuna fleece consists of a very fine down mixed with coarser guard hair, both alpha-keratin fibers with a scaled cuticle over a cortex, and the down must be separated from the hair before spinning. Fineness is the basis of its value, but no single diameter figure is asserted here, because published values vary with population and measurement method; buyers should ask for laboratory measurement of the lot. The fiber is also chemically distinctive: ambient-ionization mass spectrometry of fleece showed species-specific profiles dominated by fatty acids, cholesterol and related compounds, which the authors attributed mainly to genetics rather than diet.
vicuna.process: Harvest follows the chaku (also written chaccu), an ancestral Andean practice of rounding up wild vicunas, shearing them and releasing them. Studies in Argentina recorded raised cortisol, glucose, heart rate and vigilance during capture and handling, changes judged physiologically tolerated, and a Peruvian study found no difference in the proportion of young born to shorn and unshorn females after spring shearing. Animals with sarcoptic mange cannot be shorn. The fleece is then dehaired and cleaned, often by hand; in one documented artisanal shawl, dehairing and cleaning made up about half of a roughly 3,300 US dollar cost, before spinning, twisting, loom weaving and finishing.
vicuna.performance: Vicuna down shares the hygroscopic, self-extinguishing and acid-dyeable behavior of keratin fibers, but it is usually sold in its natural color and handled as a luxury fiber. Very fine fibers in soft, lightly twisted yarns make fabrics that are pleasant to touch but vulnerable to abrasion and pilling at friction points, and any guard hair left after dehairing reduces softness, which is why dehairing quality matters so much. Like all protein fibers it must be protected from clothes moth and carpet beetle larvae and washed gently, if at all.
vicuna.identify: Burn tests (indicative only, and to be done with care) show keratin behavior and cannot identify species. Morphological hair analysis does not resolve camelid species reliably, and in a study by the US National Fish and Wildlife Forensic Laboratory, infrared spectroscopy identified alpaca but could not separate vicuna from guanaco. Direct-analysis-in-real-time mass spectrometry separated vicuna, guanaco and alpaca fleece with 99.9% cross-validated accuracy and correctly assigned blind samples, a tool for enforcement against poached fiber. ATR-FTIR with chemometrics has also discriminated vicuna among eight commercial animal fibers.
vicuna.labeling: In the US, vicuna is one of the specialty fibers the Wool Products Labeling Act of 1939 brings within the definition of wool, so the name vicuna may be used with its percentage. In the EU, Annex I of Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 lists vicuna among the named fine animal hairs. International trade depends on CITES: an earlier listing that barred commercial trade helped populations recover, and some national populations have since been listed so that fiber shorn from live animals can be traded under conditions. Trade in shorn fiber and cloth must be checked against the current listing, any annotation and the country of origin. Buyers should ask for origin and CITES documentation for the specific item.
vicuna.past: The vicuna's modern history is a conservation case study. After centuries of hunting, a captive breeding program began in Argentina at the end of the 1960s under INTA, the national agricultural technology institute, and CITES restrictions on commercial fiber trade let wild numbers recover before live-shorn fiber trade was reopened for some populations. Live shearing for export was then promoted to give Andean communities income and to make shorn animals worthless to poachers; the fiber fetched about 566 US dollars per kilogram in 2004. Tensions remain: modelers showed that legal markets can also create demand for poached fiber, a 2022 study reported falling raw-fiber prices, and sarcoptic mange, at up to 60% prevalence in some populations, threatens herds and harvests.
